Time integration exposes a second limitation: a natural weighted forcing bound can remain small while the gap-transport multiplier grows arbitrarily large in the scalar model. The manuscript remains unchanged. Chat0002 is recorded and refreshed; capture of this final reply is queued.
Perhaps the BBGKY hierarchy truncation ideas might be more relevant here. We looked into that previously, but now that we have another hierarchy it might be useful again.
I’ll find the earlier BBGKY work and compare its truncation assumptions with the new S/T hierarchy, focusing on whether it offers a controlled remainder or a useful signed estimate.

The earlier work treated the omitted hierarchy as a response with memory. The new S/T system gives us something more concrete: truncating at order \(P\) leaves explicit forcing in just the last two even and odd equations, and the collar bounds make those omitted moments decay geometrically with \(P\). The key question is whether the finite system keeps that error small during evolution.

A concrete alternative has emerged: build the retained moments from a finite canonical zero product and evolve that polynomial by the exact heat equation. This keeps the moments mutually consistent and offers a specific route to a uniform error bound over the given time interval. I’m recording it as the next proof task; it is not yet an established approximation theorem or a stronger signed bound.

Yes. **The new hierarchy makes the truncation question considerably more concrete.** I found the earlier Jacobi-tail/memory discussion and compared it with the S/T equations.

Two useful findings emerged:

- Truncating at order \(P\) leaves explicit errors in only the last two even and odd equations. The collar bounds make those errors geometrically small.
- Small boundary errors alone do not guarantee accurate evolution: the straightforward absolute-error propagation develops factorial amplification. This limits that particular error estimate; it does not establish instability of the actual truncation.

I recommend testing a closure whose moments come from an **actual finite canonical zero product evolved by the exact heat equation**. That preserves their mutual consistency—a central concern in the [BBGKY study we previously consulted](https://arxiv.org/html/1204.4395v1). There is a concrete route to bounding its error throughout the independently established tube, including mergers.

This requires finite initial divisor information; it is not yet a closure determined by a few low moments, nor a stronger signed bound.

I saved the [comparison and derivations](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/notes/15_VCD_GT_CM_B05_BBGKY_TRUNCATION_RECONSIDERATION_20261118.md), updated progress, and refreshed chat history.

**Next: [E] E16 — Sol:** prove the common-time approximation and its moment/transport error bounds using the [frozen contract](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/research-progress/handoffs/VCD-GT-CM-E16-r1.md).

One more thing, I think we can also assume that the pair under consideration is the closest of any neighboring zeros. That assumption is reasonable, because if it isn't then we can instead focus on the pair that is.
I’ll check how a closest-pair choice fits the moving count-two tube, especially whether it gives useful exterior spacing and whether the same pair remains selected during the evolution.

Choosing a closest pair works at a fixed time in a finite window. It does not automatically give the same choice throughout a moving tube, and the closest pair can be real even when a nonreal pair exists elsewhere. I’m recording the spacing bounds that minimality genuinely gives, while keeping the tube and pair-selection requirements explicit.

There might be a more statistical way of looking at it. We could consider the evolution of the closest pair in a statistical sense, so it could be the closest pair in some region, and see how that evolves for a short period of time. This could possibly help understand the statistics of the pair distances better, or bound them in some way. In principle this could help lower the De Bruijn Newman constant, because at one point we know all of the zeros are real, and these types of arguments could extend down.

That gives a concrete statistical formulation: average over a moving height window and follow its smallest gap for a short time. I’ll connect it to the earlier pair-statistics work and the backward gap equation, then check what kind of statistical bound could support a lower upper bound on the de Bruijn–Newman constant.

There is a useful quantitative foothold here: before the first collision, the real exterior zeros give a short-time safety estimate using the initial gap and its two neighboring gaps. That makes joint three-gap statistics a concrete target. I’m checking the proof and the coverage needed to turn that estimate into a bound on Λ.

The estimate gives a concrete improvement: when the target gap and its two neighboring gaps are all \(g\), it guarantees safety for a backward interval shorter than \(g^2/6\), compared with \(g^2/8\) from the gap alone. To improve an upper bound on Λ, we would still need to rule out every exceptional pair and cover all heights. I’m having the comparison checked separately.

The separate check found no formula error. It identified two clarifications: keep the estimate within the heat-time interval covered by the existing proofs, and correct a source reference. I’m making those changes. The remaining research question is whether the canonical three-gap distribution can give a sufficiently strong bound on the rare unsafe configurations.

The corrected comparison passed the internal review. It also confirms a useful limitation: when a gap is much smaller than both neighbors, the improvement is slight. That makes the joint statistics near exceptionally small gaps the important target. I’m saving the result, review, and next research question in the investigation records.

Yes—the regional formulation lets us follow the minimum gap even when the minimizing pair changes. I developed it into an evolution law and a useful conditional estimate.

The strongest concrete finding uses **three consecutive initial gaps**: the target gap and its two neighbors. When all three equal \(g\), the neighboring zeros improve the backward allowance from
\[
\Delta<g^2/8 \quad\text{to}\quad \Delta<g^2/6,
\]
within the stated first-collision argument. The improvement becomes small when the target gap is much narrower than its neighbors.

This connects directly to your BBGKY suggestion: the minimum-gap distribution depends on the pair’s surrounding zeros. Joint gap statistics therefore offer more information than the minimum distribution alone.

To lower an **upper bound on Λ**, the statistical estimate must eliminate every exceptional collision and cover unbounded heights. That step remains open; no improved Λ bound is claimed.

The new proofs are taking shape. The manuscript now distinguishes exact infinite hierarchy closure, a geometrically small truncation residual whose stability still needs control, and the backward three-gap comparison. I’ve also added the joint forcing and deflated-derivative results so the statistical direction follows from the earlier theory.

The expanded draft compiles cleanly to 38 pages. The separate reviewer has checked the new algebra without finding a formula error and is now checking assumptions and transitions across the assembled paper. I’m reviewing the rendered pages for layout, references, and equation readability.

The review identified three small clarifications: require a heat-flow slice when stating a time derivative, define the minimum for windows with fewer than two zeros, and make the approximation’s reality assumption explicit.
